# Issues

**The register of everything open in this repo.** Defects, gaps, and questions
awaiting a ruling. One id per item, stable forever.

**This file is the source of truth for what is open.** Nothing is open unless it
is here. Other documents no longer carry their own open-item lists — they link
here. Long analysis may stay where it was argued (`packages/*/PROJECT_STATE.md`,
`IDEAS/*.md`); the **Detail** column points at it. What must
never happen again is an item existing in exactly one document that nobody reads.

**What belongs here:** shipped behavior that is wrong, a gap that blocks
something, a question that needs a decision. **What does not:** features and
roadmap (`IDEAS/`), settled rulings (`DECISIONS.md`), traps that are correct
behavior you must know about (`CLAUDE.md` § Live hazards), history
(`packages/*/CHANGES.md`).

**Closed items age out to [ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md).**
§ Closed below keeps the recent ones; the archive keeps the rest, verbatim.
Together they hold every id ever issued, and an id is never reused — so a
`FJS-###` named in a comment, a handoff, or a package file resolves in exactly
one of the two files. Search both before concluding an id is unknown.

## Conventions

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Id** | `FJS-###` for a defect or gap, `FJS-D##` for a decision. **Never reused, never renumbered.** Closing an item moves it to § Closed with its id. |
| **Sev** | `S1` blocker — data loss, a security hole, or cannot ship · `S2` high — silently wrong, costs a day to find · `S3` medium · `S4` low or cosmetic |
| **Status** | `open` — verified open on the date shown · `stale?` — inherited from an older audit and **not re-verified**; probe before acting · `contested` — the recorded diagnosis is doubted, see the note |
| **Verified** | The date somebody last ran it. A `stale?` row's date is when it was *written*, not confirmed. |

**A row has exactly the columns its table's header names**, and `fli
register:check` fails on anything else (`row-shape`). Both ways of getting it
wrong are silent: a row with FEWER columns is one pasted from the other table,
and the reader infers a shape from the cell count, so it is given a status
nobody wrote and no other rule can see it; a row with MORE has the excess
**dropped when the file is rendered** — in § Closed that is the *How* column, so
the row displays with no citations while they sit in the file. Links belong
inside the last declared column, joined with ` · `, and a `|` that is part of a
sentence is escaped `\|`.

`stale?` is load-bearing. The eight rows inherited from the 2026-07-31 audit
(now `IDEAS/coherence-review.md`) were re-probed on 2026-08-10 and **five of the eight were wrong**:
two were already fixed (conduit's secrets, `admin:generate`), one was never
reproducible (conduit's version skew), and two were right about a defect and
wrong about what it was — sierra's prefetch is not an auth *bypass* but a
cached 401, and caravan's row named three bugs of which two were fixed.
**Treat a `stale?` row as a lead, not a fact** (`VERIFYING.md`).

**The register also goes stale in the closing direction, which nothing here was
watching for.** `FJS-043` was fixed in the tree with a comment describing the
old defect in the past tense, and stayed `open` for eight days because closing
is a second action nobody owed. A row's `Verified` date is evidence about when
somebody last *looked*, not about whether the defect survives — 22 rows carried
`open` at 2026-08-02 when this audit ran, which is the same fiction `stale?`
exists to name, wearing the other label.

| <a id="fjs-846"></a>FJS-846 | mesa | **An instance `<script>` does not run in source order: every `class` and `function` declaration is moved to the end, so a `const` above a `class` throws TDZ at mount.** The emitter splits the script into variable declarations, topologically sorted by dependency, and everything else, then emits the variables first. A `class` declaration is in the rest and a `const` that instantiates it is in the variables, so the component throws `Cannot access 'C' before initialization` on its first mount with nothing warning. The comment at the end of the statement loop says function declarations hoist so order does not matter, which is true of `function` and false of `class`. The general form is worse: arbitrary statement order is not preserved, measured with a call before a `const` emitted after it. Finding `script-3` of the [Mesa audit](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/05d792af-815d-4b4b-b2d8-9c9cb21efabe). **Narrowed 2026-09-05**: the CLASS half is closed. A class is a declaration and declarations here are already ordered by dependency, so classes joined the same topological sort rather than staying in the trailing loop — `classDeclTimeRefs()` collects only what the declaration EVALUATES (superclass, computed keys, static fields and blocks), because a method body is deferred and orders nothing, and ordering on every identifier would turn `class R { read() { return n } }` into a cycle and refuse a working component. A genuine cycle is now reported naming both sides. **What remains is the general reorder**: an expression statement before a later `const` still runs after it. Measured across the corpus before deciding — **82 of 331 instance scripts** have that shape and nearly all are harmless, since a `const` over a reactive `let` is a memo and re-derives — so a warning there would be noise rather than a diagnostic, and the honest state is a stated limitation rather than a shipped warning nobody can act on. | Id | Area | Question | Detail |

| <a id="fjs-d121"></a>FJS-D121 | litestone · sierra | **Does a per-caller ORDER belong in the schema — the third value-set axis?** Axis 3 of `IDEAS/value-sets.md`, held out of `FJS-D120` deliberately and WANTED, not parked. The case is the one this whole line of work started from: assigning a task, a person picks the same one to three people over and over, and an alphabetical list makes them search every time. Float the ones they actually use. Mozilla calls the general shape *frecency*; a sliding window gives decay for free. **It is not membership and must not be fused with strength.** A *suggested* binding and a *suggested* order are different sentences, and a system with one word for both cannot say *anyone may be assigned, but show me the three I actually use*. Nothing about order changes what is legal. **What makes it a question rather than a build**: it needs somewhere to KEEP the recency, and that is per-caller state rather than a fact about the data — so unlike membership and strength it is not obviously a schema declaration at all. Three shapes were considered: a `Recent` model (its own table, `Int @id` — see `packages/litestone/docs/modeling.md`), a JSON field on `User`, and localStorage. The argument FOR declaring it here anyway is the one that put the control table in one module: a hand-written picker and a generated one must not order differently. The argument AGAINST is that it is per-caller and non-authoritative, which is the definition of a UI-realm concern. A ruling has to say where the counter lives, whether the schema names it at all, and whether `resource.options()` applies it or a control does. | [value-sets.md](IDEAS/value-sets.md) § open questions · [FJS-D120](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d120) |
| <a id="fjs-d122"></a>FJS-D122 | litestone · sierra | **How does a DEPENDENT set compose — one whose members depend on another field's value?** The second axis held out of `FJS-D120`, and WANTED. Pick a country, then the state list is that country's. Pick a category, then the subcategory list narrows. Salesforce calls it a controlling field, Frappe a Dynamic Link. **The prior art is a warning rather than a model**: dependent picklists are the one feature Salesforce could not compose with global value sets, which is the exact shape `FJS-D120` just adopted — so taking their mechanism wholesale imports the incompatibility. Two halves and they may want different answers. The DATA half is a `where` that reads a sibling column, which the `@@allow` expression language can nearly say already (`@@scope` is a predicate over the row, and `@derived` reads this row's own columns) — the open part is whether the sibling being read is the value ON the record or the value currently in the FORM, which are different rows on a create. The UI half is a picker that reloads when its controlling field changes and clears a value the new list no longer contains, which touches `resource.options()`'s cache key and `$context.form`. A ruling has to say whether the dependency is declared on the set or on the binding, and what happens to a stored value that a later change to the controlling field makes illegal — refuse the write, clear the field, or leave it and report. | [value-sets.md](IDEAS/value-sets.md) § open questions · [FJS-D120](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d120) |
| <a id="fjs-d118"></a>FJS-D118 | sierra | **Does a page state where *back* goes, and if so is it an attribute?** The sibling of [FJS-D115](#fjs-d115) and deliberately not ruled with it. `KOBAMI/my.maid.tech` writes `data-return` in the same shape as `data-confirm` — an attribute, one delegated listener — to stash the path a create or edit page should return to, so a form reached from three places goes back to the right one. The mechanism looks identical and the OWNER is not: a confirmation is a UI affordance and belongs to the kit, while *where does back go* is navigation, which is `@frontierjs/sierra`'s router — the only thing that knows the history stack, the route table and whether the previous entry is even this app. Putting it on the kit's listener would make `@frontierjs/ui` reach for a router it does not depend on. What a ruling has to settle: whether the state lives in `history.state` (survives a reload, dies on a fresh tab), in the URL as a `?return=` (shareable, and a caller-supplied path is an open redirect the moment it is followed without checking), or in a store (cheapest, gone on reload); and whether an attribute is the right surface at all when the router could answer it from the route table without anybody writing anything | [IDEAS/app-conventions-audit.md](IDEAS/app-conventions-audit.md) § 3.1 · [FJS-D115](#fjs-d115) · [sierra router](packages/sierra/src/router/index.js) |
| <a id="fjs-d117"></a>FJS-D117 | sierra · cli | **Does a co-located route part carry its folder in its NAME, and does `fli check` grade it?** Sierra already rules the roles — `index.mesa` routes, `_module.mesa` is the layout, `_prefix` and PascalCase are co-located components — and says nothing about what those components are CALLED. maid.tech adds the discipline on top: `_Plural.mesa` is the reusable collection panel imported cross-route, `_plural.Thing.mesa` is the folder-scoped part. What it buys is that an import list is readable without paths and a flat search is unambiguous, instead of twelve files named `List.mesa`. **The same app measures how it fails**, which is the substance of the question: a fork keeps the old prefix, so `routes/contacts/` holds four byte-identical copies of `routes/clients/` files still named `_clients.*`, and `routes/messages/` is a fork of `routes/notes/` still named `_notes.*` — at which point the prefix, the one thing that made the convention worth having, is lying. So the convention is worth little stated and a lot checked: *a `_prefix.Part.mesa` whose prefix does not match its folder* is a cheap rule in `core/checks.js`, which already owns everything derived from the file tree, and it catches the exact failure that was measured. So **reuse costs a second compiler backend emitting a cell tree, not a renderer**, which is more than it looked like before anyone counted; every Mesa target that exists produces markup, SSR and `email-kit`'s `target: 'email'` included, so nothing in the tree says a non-markup target is cheap. | <a id="fjs-d25"></a>FJS-D25 | css | **Ship `Lead` and `Kicker` as terms?** Both are concepts the package already names in `tokens.css` and then provides no way to write. `--text-lg` is commented "**lead paragraph**" and `--text-2xs` is "**the uppercase overline**" — the rungs are tuned for these two jobs and neither has a class, so every consumer hand-rolls one. **Lead**: the standfirst under a page title — larger than body, muted, held to a measure. Three implementations, one idea, no name is the condition that produces exactly that drift. Not to be confused with `.sg-h1`, which is a display treatment (44px/500/serif vs the h1 rung's 36px/700) and is legitimately the guide's own | [packages/css/guide/guide.js](packages/css/guide/guide.js) § pageHeader() · [packages/css/src/foundation/tokens.css](packages/css/src/foundation/tokens.css) § type scale · [packages/css/vocabulary.js](packages/css/vocabulary.js) |

| Id | Title | Closed | How |
| <a id="fjs-884"></a>FJS-884 | mesa — **The watch proxy answered structural questions with the wrong mechanism, and every rule about it had been learned in one direction.** | 2026-09-06 | Closed across two passes; the identity half went with [FJS-849](#fjs-849). The four that remained: **A symbol-keyed write and delete fired nothing** — not even the whole-object watch, which the same write with a STRING key wakes. A symbol is not a change at a path, since it cannot be a watch segment and reading one subscribes to nothing; it is still a change to the object, so it now fires the node and its ancestors and nothing narrower. **The first measurement of this was wrong**: a bare `watchProxy` has no declared watches and therefore fires for no key at all, string or symbol, so the probe showed a gap that was not there. The real comparison needs `watchPath(p, '')` declared, and then string and symbol differ exactly as reported. **A frozen nested object** came back as the native `Cannot assign to read only property 'b' of object '#<Object>'` — the property, and nothing about where it sits. Now names the path, says the object is frozen, and keeps the original as `cause`. Svelte met the same class from the other side and removed its on-target symbol to escape it ([#11887](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/11887), [PR #12916](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/pull/12916)). **A write from inside a derivation** is warned about, not refused. A memo is lazy, so a derivation written for its side effect stops the moment nothing reads it — silently. Svelte refuses it outright (`state_unsafe_mutation`), but a write from inside `fn()` to one of the memo's OWN dependencies is a HANDLED case here that `_recompute` clears `dirty` before running for, and refusing would contradict behavior this runtime documents. **Measured before choosing**: instrumented across the mesa, sierra and ui suites, nothing in this repo writes from inside a derivation at all. **`structuredClone` has no fix and the row now says so.** The get trap must return a proxy or there is no reactivity below the first level, so `{...state}` hands back proxies and the clone throws `DataCloneError`. `unproxy()` is the answer, it works, and `VISION.md` mentioned it **zero times** — the answer existed and was undiscoverable. Documented beside RULE 49, along with the symbol rule. 6 red of 12 · [runtime.js](packages/mesa/src/runtime.js) · [watch-proxy-writes.test.js](packages/mesa/test/watch-proxy-writes.test.js) · [VISION.md](packages/mesa/docs/VISION.md) |
| <a id="fjs-885"></a>FJS-885 | mesa — **An attribute had one owner and three writers, and the one the compiler picked decided whether a rule applied.** | 2026-09-06 | All three named findings closed. **Two `on:click` on one element silently kept only the last.** A delegated handler is a PROPERTY — `el.__click = fn` — so the second overwrote the first and it fired never, and only on that path: the non-delegated branch calls `addEvent`, which appends, so the same markup behaved differently depending on whether the event carried a modifier. `mergeEvents` already existed. The merge is emitted only for the SECOND and later handler, so ordinary output is unchanged. Svelte attaches both and fires both ([#2688](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/2688), [#128](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/128)), which is what the neighbouring path here already did. 3 red, 3 controls. **A custom element handed an object got `[object Object]`.** `set_attribute` read a fixed HTML name list where the spread path next door asks the ELEMENT. Narrowed to a NON-PRIMITIVE on a custom element that declares the property — the one case where an attribute cannot carry the value and the element has already answered by defining it. A string still goes to the attribute, so a `[foo="bar"]` selector keeps matching: Svelte prefers the property whenever one exists, carries open reports from both directions ([#12624](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/12624), [#15455](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/15455)) and had to force `spellcheck` and `translate` BACK to `setAttribute` ([#12734](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/pull/12734)). Where it still stringifies, it now warns once per element-name and attribute — but only when the result is literally `[object Object]`, so a `Date` is left alone. **`xlink:`/`xml:` were written as literal colon names in no namespace.** `setAttributeNS` now, and **the assertion is in the BROWSER drive** because happy-dom normalizes the colon form into the namespace by itself — under it the fix and its absence are indistinguishable and the first version of this test passed for the wrong reason. 4 red in real Chrome; the three that pass are the controls, including an invented `foo:bar` prefix that must stay in no namespace · [compiler.js](packages/mesa/src/compiler.js) · [runtime.js](packages/mesa/src/runtime.js) · [duplicate-handlers.test.js](packages/mesa/test/duplicate-handlers.test.js) · [namespaced-attributes.spec.mjs](packages/mesa/test/browser/runtime/specs/namespaced-attributes.spec.mjs) |
| <a id="fjs-935"></a>FJS-935 | litestone — **`distinct` accepted a column list, validated its names, and emitted no `DISTINCT` at all.** | 2026-09-06 | `buildSQL` reads `distinct === true` and nothing else, so `distinct: ['title']` came back as three rows over two titles — while `checkSelect` validated the array's ELEMENTS by name, so the API refused *Unknown field* and answered as though it had understood the argument. The SQL comment cost a round: a backtick in a comment inside a template literal closes the literal, and the parse error points at a line further down — the trap `CLAUDE.md` § House style already names. | <a id="fjs-898"></a>FJS-898 | junction — **Two cache drivers behind one interface disagreed twelve ways, and swapping the driver was the only way to find out** | 2026-09-05 | `batteries-9`. An interface exists so a caller need not know which backend answers, and every difference here was a way that promise was false — measured before anything changed: a memory `get()` handed back the STORED reference (mutating the row a caller had already `set` changed what the cache held, and so did mutating what `get` answered) where sqlite round-tripped; `undefined` and a function stored in memory and threw a NOT NULL in sqlite; a **Date came back a Date from one and a string from the other**, a `Map` a `Map` and a `{}`, `NaN` itself and `null`; `clear()` answered a count and 0; `clear(pattern)` was a SUBSTRING match in memory and a PREFIX in sqlite; eviction was FIFO. **The fix is one codec both drivers call, not a fix per driver** — that is what makes a thirteenth divergence unreachable rather than unfiled. What a cache value may be is DERIVED and not chosen: JSON is what a Litestone row already is (a `DateTime` reads back an ISO string, measured), what a response body carries and what a WS frame carries, so the cache holds what the wire holds and owes no rule of its own. What JSON would LOSE is refused at `set()` naming the key and the way out — a Date says store the ISO string, a BigInt says store digits the way `Int @big` crosses — and the walk is the one `JSON.stringify` was already doing, so grading costs no second pass. `undefined` is refused for a second reason: `get()` answers it for a miss, so a stored one could not be read back, which is also what makes `getOrSet`'s miss check sound. **The memory driver holds the value ENCODED**, which is what buys value semantics: a shared reference is a semantics no persistent backend can offer, so code written against it breaks on the day the driver is swapped. Eviction is LRU with `get()` a use and `has()` deliberately not one, an overwrite re-inserting because `Map.set` on an existing key does not move it. `getOrSet` is the read-through with single flight — one factory run per key however many callers arrive, a rejection reaching all of them and cached for none. **The conformance suite is the artefact and it found the twelfth on its first run**: sqlite escaped `%` and `_` with a backslash and declared no `ESCAPE`, so a prefix containing either matched nothing. It also retired a workaround — `buildCacheHooks` was `structuredClone`-ing on both store and read because the interface promised nothing, a second answer to isolation that could not be true of a driver it has never heard of. **Measured**: a 20-row `find` result costs ~70µs to encode and ~31µs to read against ~73µs for the `structuredClone` the hook paid TWICE, so the service cache is a wash on store and ~2.3x faster on read; a session-sized value is 1.8µs and 0.7µs against 0.7µs. **`verifySession` is deliberately not cached**: a revoked session would go on working for the TTL, which is a security property traded for an indexed read, and `client.auth` calls `POST /auth/logout` precisely so the row stops being valid. Load-bearing, each stubbed: 24 of 74 fail without the codec, 2 without single flight, 1 each without LRU, the prefix, the count and the `ESCAPE`. | <a id="fjs-703"></a>FJS-703 | junction · sierra — **Presence was unconditional, could not be turned off, and was O(N²), so a reconnect storm was not survivable** | 2026-09-03 | Finding `realtime-6` of the [API-realm audit](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/afba85f4-efe9-4959-92ca-a1b010dd2a16). **Two fixes answering different halves.** `channels(setup, { presence })` is `false` by default — `true` or a list of names and `prefix:*` patterns turns it on — which removes the cost entirely from every app that does not use a feature every channel was paying for; a list is the shape to reach for, since presence belongs on the one channel a room is and never on the ten a data-sync app announces model writes over. And the payload is **byte-identical** across envelope versions, so a value written before this change reads `v1d.<p>` where the operand encodes `v2d.<kid>.<p>`: every deterministic and `@hashed` lookup **in every existing app** would have silently stopped matching, and no suite here could see it because every one builds a fresh database (`FJS-251`'s shape). `legacyForm` emits the v1 twin beside each encoding, and the pre-upgrade database is now a written test. Ruled [FJS-D183](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d183). | <a id="fjs-665"></a>FJS-665 | litestone — **The audit trail lost rows, mis-indexed them and killed writers whenever a second process touched it — and a second process is the shape the docs recommend** | 2026-09-02 | `F8` of the [foundation audit](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f629d9fc-1ae7-4aaf-b7fe-20a863c41211), the one finding of its eight that had no id. `driver logger` routes through the jsonl driver and its auto-model carries three `@@index` attributes, so every trail in every app is on the indexed path; both apps here declare it. **Three defects, all measured on the shipped code.** `statSync(f).size` then `appendFileSync` is two syscalls, so a second process appending between them made the recorded offset name the OTHER writer's line — **1,999 of 8,000, one in four**, with no artificial delay, after which an indexed read answers the wrong record with no error. | <a id="fjs-593"></a>FJS-593 | litestone — **An enum member had to be a legal identifier, so a closed set written for a person to read could not be expressed at all** | 2026-08-29 | `enum S { Draft }` parsed and `enum S { "On Hold" }` did not. Prisma's `@map` on the member is the other one and buys a separate code-name at the price of a bidirectional layer on every read and write, which nothing in the corpus asks for; `@label` already covers display, so the code-name would be a third thing. | <a id="fjs-575"></a>FJS-575 | litestone — **`@scale` caps at 9 places and usage-based billing writes 15 — but the cap was never the binding constraint, and raising it would have made things worse** | 2026-08-29 | The row asked for a bigger cap. A **rate** is small-magnitude and many-placed, and `@scale(9)` holds every rate in the 25 columns found across lago, discourse and triggerdev. A **precise accumulated total** is big-magnitude *and* many-placed, fits no 64-bit integer at any useful scale, and is an un-rounded intermediate rather than a stored quantity — so where it lives is rounding and allocation, which is [`FJS-D154`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d154), since ruled. | <a id="fjs-573"></a>FJS-573 | cli — **A crashed deploy stranded its lock, and the pid recorded in it was the pid of a shell that had already exited — so nothing could tell a stale lock from a live one, and the resume the journal was offering could only be reached by deleting a file by hand** | 2026-08-29 | Ruled rather than patched ([FJS-D156](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d156)): the journal owns *what state did the last run leave*, the lock owns *is another run working here*, and the lock only ever looked like a second answer to the first because it could not expire. A better pid was not available and never could be — `fli` runs on the operator's machine and reaches the target one command at a time, so **there is no process on the target to point at**. So the lock records what is true: the run, who started it, when, and **which step it is inside** — the fact that makes the duration beside it mean something, since four minutes in `04-build-api` is a build and four minutes in `06-swap` is a run that died. The step comes from a `beforeStep` announcement in the step runner, which is the only place it can: the build is the longest thing a deploy does and runs BEFORE the journal opens (`04c-journal`), and a timer cannot serve it because `execSync` blocks the loop for the whole of a step. Neither register judges liveness — that is a fact about a process this machine cannot see — so the refusal reports and names both ways out: **`fli deploy --resume`** continues what the journal holds and takes the lock over, **`fli deploy:unlock`** drops it and starts fresh. A resume was always safe without a probe (a succeeded step replays into a no-op, a step is claimed compare-and-set, and different bytes are a different Release and therefore a new transition); the lock was only what made it unreachable. A TTL was considered and refused — the heartbeat can only tick per step, so the TTL would have to exceed the longest build. One format, one parser, four scripts, three readers (`core/lock.js`) where each of `deploy`, `deploy:status` and `deploy:doctor` used to `cat` the file and read it its own way — `deploy:status` split `<pid>:<iso>:<target>` on `:` and had been reading the hour as the timestamp for its whole life. | <a id="fjs-569"></a>FJS-569 | litestone · junction — **`busy_timeout` was set on four SQLite connections and absent from four others — and the number was a literal an app could not change** | 2026-08-29 | **`busy_timeout` is set on four SQLite connections and missing from four others, so which databases wait under contention is an accident of which file opened them.** Measured 2026-08-29 with two connections, one holding the write lock: with `busy_timeout = 5000` the second waits 5007ms; **with no pragmas at all it fails in 1ms**. Two things fell out: `MESSAGE_KEYWORDS` had claimed `time: ['format']` for as long as the emitter produced no format, so an author’s `@time(message:)` was keyed to a keyword no consumer could ever check; and the seconds variant was two alternative regexes where one optional group says the same thing — the flag WIDENS what may be stored and does not make a finer value mandatory. **Still nothing in this repo declares one**: `example` and `basecamp` hold 141 `DateTime` columns and zero `@time`, `@date` or `@datetime`, so this is covered by unit tests on both sides of the wire and by no drive. 19 cases in `test/time-column.test.ts`, 3 in sierra’s `form-fields`; litestone 3136 pass, sierra 1144 pass. | <a id="fjs-518"></a>FJS-518 | junction · sierra · jetty — **A record read with `get(id)` is a dead object, so every detail screen in the repo goes stale the moment somebody else writes the row.** The live path is the LIST path and only the list path: `client.resource()` opens the socket, wires `created`/`patched`/`removed` into a `Store`, and decides membership and position per event. The framework's headline guarantee is that you never invalidate, because the server says what changed; on a detail screen that guarantee is simply false, and it is false in the silent-wrong-data class — the page renders, the numbers are stale, nothing throws. **Two rows of one model can also disagree with each other**: the store is per-`resource()` call (`const store = new Store<T>()` inside `resource()`), so two `createResource('orders')` in two route files are two copies, kept in step only because both subscribe to the same service. Nothing keys a row to an identity, which is also why nothing can mark a value provisional or put one back — the reason no optimistic update exists anywhere in the repo. **Ruled 2026-08-25 rather than patched**: a node per row keyed by model, a list as a view over it, a detail as a view of one, a TTL for lifetime, and an overlay carrying intent — [FJS-D138](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d138), which carries the build order. jetty's copy of the store is the same defect one package over ([FJS-493](#fjs-493)) and is fixed by importing rather than by a second repair. **Fixed 2026-08-25**, as `FJS-D138` sequenced it. `packages/junction/src/client/nodes.ts` is the registry — one node per row, keyed by MODEL and by a normalized id, because a list holds `{ id: 5 }` and a detail screen is reached by a URL carrying `'5'`, and two nodes there means the push moves exactly one of them. `Store` is a VIEW now: bound it holds ids and materialises through the registry, so `store.get()` still answers rows and **no screen changed** — `useStore` is the one bridge to a Mesa signal and nothing in either app calls `subscribe` or `get` directly. Unbound it is what it always was, which is what the fifteen `Store` cases in `client.test.ts` are the negative control for. Lifetime is a **TTL** (`nodeTtlMs`, default 30s) rather than a reference count the application maintains, which is the part of Apollo and Relay everyone complains about. `resource.record(id)` is the view of one; Sierra's wraps it so the first read goes through the resource's own `_call('get')` — its hooks, its coercion, its `@version` — while Junction keeps the rule about WHEN to read. **A push moves the value and does not move the remembered version**, which is `FJS-341` restated as a test: the node is the synced truth and the view is what this screen READ. `example`'s order detail is the first caller and its two manual `await load()` after an action are gone — that reload was the app hiding this. **Proven in a browser**: `verify:live` gained a third question (17 assertions, up from 14) — a watcher tab on the detail page, the order paid from node over HTTP on a session of its own, the status moving with `sameDocument: true`. Negative-controlled: reverted to `service.get(id)` it reads `{"status":"pending","moved":false}`. Two things fell out on the way: `remove` drops `$withDeleted`, so the drive could not clean up after itself and had only ever passed on a fresh seed ([FJS-523](#fjs-523)); and jetty's copy is untouched by design — it gets this by importing rather than by a second repair ([FJS-493](#fjs-493)). | <a id="fjs-525"></a>FJS-525 | caravan — **a fixed-time schedule fired zero times in spring and twice in autumn** | 2026-08-25 | The firing path asked *does the current minute match*, which on the two days a year when the local clock is not a function of real time gave two wrong answers. Measured on `America/New_York` before the fix: `30 2 * * *` fired **0** times on 2026-03-08 because 02:30 never occurred, and `30 1 * * *` fired **2** times on 2026-11-01 as two dispatch ids, since `occurrenceKey('cron', name, minute)` was built from the epoch minute and the two 01:30s are different epoch minutes. **Fixed by walking the local clock instead of sampling it** (`FJS-D144`, Vixie cron's rule): a fixed-time schedule keeps a mark — the last wall-clock minute it looked at — and each tick walks FORWARD from that mark to now, firing every minute the expression matches. No manifest key, no language change, no parser — a line scan over a file in `node_modules`, reached through that package's own `exports` map. **Fixed 2026-08-24** as `fli check`'s twenty-seventh rule, `package-model-drift`. A WARNING and not an error, because a deviation can be right and the reader has to judge: both declarations are printed, and `check-baseline.json` is how an app accepts one it has argued for. **Its first run on basecamp found three things and closed all three, one of them in the package rather than the app.** (1) `User.emailVerified` and (2) `User.role` had lost `@allow('write', auth().isAdmin)` — basecamp gates update at USER(4) with `@@allow('update', id == auth().id)`, *your own row*, so the field policy is the only thing between a caller and their own `emailVerified`, and marking your own address verified is skipping the verification. **Latent rather than live**: basecamp exposes no `users` service and its gate grades on `status` and `WorkspaceMember.role`, neither of which is this — it becomes real the day a profile screen writes through a service over `db.user`. Both restored, and both now appear in `db/access.snapshot.md`, so a future removal is a diff. (3) `User.accountId` was `String?` against auth's `Int?` — and here the PACKAGE was wrong: every id `@frontierjs/auth` declares is a uuid, so an `Int?` could not hold one, which is what made the column unusable for the one app that reached for it. auth ships `String?` now; `SessionContext.accountId` was always a string either way. Seven cases in `tests/checks.test.js`, mutation-checked both directions — never comparing, and comparing the APP's columns instead of the package's (the false-positive shape), each turn it red. Green: cli 848, auth 244, basecamp 143 + 301/301 · [checks.js](packages/cli/core/checks.js) · [checks.test.js](packages/cli/tests/checks.test.js) · [user.lite](packages/auth/db/user.lite) · [schema.lite](packages/basecamp/db/schema.lite) |

The test must PARSE the emitted output, not merely assert a clean compile; asserting the compile is what let this run. Filed S3 rather than S2 because the trigger requires the author to pick one of nine specific names; the cost once triggered is S2-shaped — silent at compile, loud and misdirected at runtime · **Fixed 2026-08-23.** `BUILTIN_LOCALS` names the thirteen injected names beside `RESERVED_WORDS`, and `analyzeScript` walks its own `ast.body` — not `vars`, which carries neither function nor class declarations, both of which collided — refusing every declaration form by name. It THROWS rather than pushing to `errors`, because the call site downgrades that whole array to warnings and a module that does not parse is not a warning. Scoped to the factory, so a nested `const $props` is still legal; over-refusing there would break code that never collided. Verified 65/65 refusals across five declaration forms including destructuring, with eight controls still compiling and parsing. Seven cases added to `test/emission.test.js`. Green: mesa 1233 vitest + 82 runtime-browser + 47 vite-browser, `@frontierjs/ui` 857 with 69/69 components opened. The surface was found to be 13 names rather than the 9 first measured — `$inspect` collides only when `debug !== false`, and `$ctxProvide`/`$ctxRead` only where `$context` is in use, which is why the reserved set is keyed off what the compiler MAY inject rather than what a given config does inject · [compiler.js](packages/mesa/src/compiler.js) · [emission.test.js](packages/mesa/test/emission.test.js) · [FJS-D132](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d132) · [IDEAS/mesa-dollar-namespace.md](IDEAS/mesa-dollar-namespace.md) |

| <a id="fjs-367"></a>FJS-367 | junction — **the shipped `paginate()` hook was inert in every app, and the fix is that it stops publishing a second copy of the page** | 2026-08-21 | Measured before and after. | <a id="fjs-366"></a>FJS-366 | junction — **Every WebSocket connection was evicted after 30s, in every app, because the keepalive had a server half and no client half** | 2026-08-20 | The channels plugin evicted any connection that had not sent `{type:'ping'}` in 30s, sweeping every 10s. `JunctionClient.startHeartbeat()` sends that ping and **nothing called it** — not junction, not sierra, not `fli new`'s scaffold — so a fresh app opened a socket, received `{type:'connected'}`, and was closed with `connection evicted` ~35s later, forever. Reported from a scaffolded app; measured there as a 39.4s close and a reconnect ~1s after each. Invisible unless watched, because the socket carried no event and the reconnect succeeded: a live list simply never updated. Two things were wrong under it. **Only a ping refreshed liveness**, so a client in the middle of service calls over that same socket was evicted while plainly alive. And **the client's default interval was 30s against a 30s timeout**, so calling it would have raced the reaper anyway. Fixed by moving the drive to the SERVER — it pings an idle socket every 15s and evicts one silent for 40s, and any frame counts as liveness, malformed ones included. The client answers from its message handler rather than a timer, which is what keeps a backgrounded tab connected: browsers throttle timers to ~1/min in a hidden tab, slower than any eviction window, and a message handler is not throttled. `channels(setup, { heartbeatInterval, heartbeatTimeout })` are the knobs; `startHeartbeat()` stays for a client whose server predates this, now defaulting to 15s. `tests/heartbeat.test.ts` runs the loop against a real socket at 100ms/400ms — idle is pinged, silent is evicted, pongs hold it, ordinary traffic holds it, and the shipped client holds it with no call by the app |

| <a id="fjs-351"></a>FJS-351 | litestone — **A generated validation case did not isolate the rule it named, in both directions** | 2026-08-19 | `generateValidationCases` built every case from ONE attribute with no idea what else sat on the field. **A boundary claimed a value the field refused** — `@length(3, 200)` on an `@email` column produced `'xxx'`, so the write was refused and the runner reported *@length allows this value and the write was refused*. Measured on a six-field schema: 8 of 12 boundary cases false, 4 of 6 fields reported broken when nothing was, and the fix a reader reaches for is deleting a rule from the schema. **An invalid case was refused by somebody else's rule and counted as proof of its own** — `''` on that column is rejected by `@email`, so the two cases naming `@length` proved nothing about it. Measured by disabling `@length` in `validate.js`: on a single-rule field the runner says *the schema declares @length(3,20) and the write was ACCEPTED*, on the `@email` field it said **nothing**, and the only entries there were the two false alarms — which appear whether the rule is enforced or not, so the checker could not tell an enforced `@length` from a missing one, and the false alarm is what hid it. The same measurement now yields four findings, all naming `@length`, and zero on a schema with nothing wrong with it. `attempt()` also carried the message every case declared and never compared it; it does now, as a backstop for an implementation refusing for a reason the schema did not predict. Both closed against one judge: `validateField` is now exported from `core/validate.js` — the function that decides this on a real write — because a table of formats in the generator would be a second definition of every rule. **It is asked about the field's OTHER rules only**: whether a value satisfies or breaks the rule it NAMES is established by construction, and asking the implementation makes the runner its own oracle — the first version did, and disabling `@length` then reported *not checked* instead of *the write was ACCEPTED*, losing the finding the runner exists to produce. Caught by measuring rather than by reasoning. **The repair is format-blind**: it grows or trims the factory's own valid sample and asks the validators, so an email grows in front of its own domain and `@startsWith("ORD-")` keeps its prefix with no code here containing either word; shrinking works on alphanumeric RUNS and leaves punctuation alone, which turns `email1@example.com` into `e@e.c` at five. Which dimension is free depends on the rule — a boundary IS its length, an invalid `@length` case need only sit outside the bound, every other rule's length is incidental. What cannot be isolated is `uncheckable`: named, with the blocking rules' own messages, because a rule that stops being asked about is this runner's failure mode one layer up — and **`litestone mutate` excludes it from the kill count**, since a row generated from the original schema appears identically under every mutant, which is the shape the 22 `error` rows had when they scored a 14-mutant schema 93%. Five tests, and basecamp's `Invitation.email` carries `@email @length(6, 200)` again — 6 rather than 5 because `a@b.c` is the shortest string `@email` accepts, so a bound at the floor is unviolatable and the runner says so |

| <a id="fjs-349"></a>FJS-349 | basecamp · conduit · junction — **The three endpoints an Outpost calls took no credential at all, and one of them redirected the fleet** | 2026-08-19 | Measured before and after, against a running API. | <a id="fjs-294"></a>FJS-294 | caravan — **Two Caravan instances on one `jobs.db` each fire every cron and each reset the other's in-flight jobs** | 2026-08-18 | The second of the two candidate answers: coordinate for real, rather than declare single ownership and refuse a second opener — a refusal would also refuse the ordinary shapes, a web process that only dispatches beside a worker that only runs, and it would state an assumption the deployment gets to make. **A running row is OWNED.** Each instance takes an id, stamps it on every row `claimNext` takes, and heartbeats into a `job_owners` table on a timer; recovery reclaims only rows whose owner has gone quiet past `lease` (30s, `heartbeat` 5s, both settable from `junction.config.js`). `markDone`/`markFailed` are guarded on the owner as well as on `running`, so a reclaimed job's late completion cannot land on the attempt that replaced it, and a clean `stop()` drops the owner row — but only with nothing in flight, since past `pool.stop()`'s deadline a handler may still be running and dropping it then invites exactly the double execution the owner prevents. **The cron half is the dedup key, not leader election**: the fire is dispatched under `cron:<job>:<epoch-minute>`, so every instance fires its own schedule and all but the first are the no-op a stated id already is (`FJS-D35`). ## See also

- `ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md` — closed rows aged out of § Closed. Same table, verbatim. Read when tracing a specific id, never cold.
- `CLAUDE.md` § Live hazards — traps that are **correct behavior**; knowing them saves a day. Not issues.
- `DECISIONS.md` — settled rulings. A `FJS-D##` closing here lands there.
- `IDEAS/` — roadmap and design records for work not started. `IDEAS/overview.md`'s wave 0 is the subset of this file that happens to be argued in an ideas file.
- `HANDOFF.md` — per-session narrative, newest first. History, not a ledger.
- `VERIFYING.md` — how to promote a `stale?` row to `open` or `closed`.
